Monday, 20 November. Radu is applying for a six-month internship at Atelier Rhône. Ioana is not taking part in the interview, to keep it fair. Nathalie receives him alone, in her office.
Good morning, Monsieur Popescu. Please, have a seat. Would you like a coffee?
Yes please, thank you. And thank you for seeing me, Madame. I know you’re very busy.
(smiles) "Monsieur Popescu", "Madame"… We’ve known each other for two years, Radu. But you’re right: today is a real interview. So, could you introduce yourself?
Of course. I’m twenty-one. I did my bachelor’s in architecture in Iași, then I came to Lyon on Erasmus. Since September I’ve been in the first year of a master’s.
Why would you like to do your internship with us, and not at a big firm?
Because I saw what you did at Fourvière. A room designed for people, not for magazines. That’s the kind of architecture I’d like to learn.
Good answer. But I’ll be direct: your sister is about to become my partner. Some people might think it’s favouritism.
I understand. That’s why I applied like everyone else, with a CV and a cover letter. And I would be grateful if you judged me on my work, not on my name.
That’s exactly what I intend to do. What are your strengths?
I draw quickly and well, by hand and on computer. I speak three languages. And I know how to work in a team: I repainted a whole studio with six people and a Spanish girl who was singing.
(laughs) I heard about that job. And your weaknesses?
I’m sometimes too impatient. And I’m not very good at painting… walls. But I learn quickly from my mistakes.
Last question. Where do you see yourself in five years?
In Lyon, if possible. With my degree, a job I enjoy, and maybe my own project. A music room in La Duchère, for example.
Good. I’ll give you my answer by Friday. Thank you, Monsieur Popescu. (quietly) And don’t say anything to your sister.

"Ahn-truh-tyan": the interview. Two nasals: "ahn" at the start, "yan" at the end.
"Say-vay": the letters C and V are read the French way.
The formal French letter has a very fixed structure. The French take it seriously, and wrong formulas make a bad impression:
Je me permets de vous écrire afin de postuler pour…
Actuellement étudiant en…, j’ai acquis une expérience de…
Je serais heureux de vous rencontrer lors d’un entretien.
Veuillez agréer, Madame, l’expression de mes salutations distinguées.
Don’t start an official letter with "Chère Madame" (too familiar), and don’t end a cover letter with "Bisous" or "Cordialement". "Cordialement" is fine for ordinary work emails.
In formal French, the conditional makes a request more polite, just as in English ("I would like", "could you"):
Je vous saurais gré de… (very formal)
"Je me permets de…" (I take the liberty of) is the favourite formula for starting a request without sounding pushy.

The advert had appeared on Atelier Rhône’s website at the beginning of November: "Seeking architecture intern, six months, from January." Radu had read it ten times. Then he had closed his computer, opened it again, and read it an eleventh time. Lucia had ended up telling him: "Apply, or stop reading it."

The problem was Ioana. Radu didn’t want his sister to help him, or even to know. "If I get it, I want it to be thanks to me," he had explained. "Not because I’m the future partner’s brother." Lucia found that very noble, and a bit silly. She had helped him anyway.

They had spent a whole weekend on the CV and the cover letter. Radu wrote the way he spoke, with lots of "super" and "great". Lucia corrected everything, sentence by sentence, like a strict schoolteacher. "A cover letter isn’t a message to your mates," she kept saying. "You say ’Madame’, not ’Hi’."

The hardest part had been the closing formula. Radu didn’t understand why you had to write such a long sentence to say goodbye. "Please accept, Madam, the expression of my distinguished greetings? Nobody talks like that!" Lucia had shrugged. "In France they do. On paper, anyway."

He had sent his application the following Monday, at six in the morning, so as not to change his mind. Three days later he had received a very formal email: "Sir, we have received your application and would like to invite you to an interview on Monday 20 November at 10 a.m. Kind regards, Nathalie Fabre, director."

Radu had burst out laughing when he read the message. Nathalie Fabre had known him for two years. She had danced with him at Ioana’s wedding. She had seen him knock a pot of yellow paint over his feet. And now she was writing "Sir" to him. Then he understood: it was exactly what he had asked for.

To prepare for the interview, he went to see Odile. For forty years she had recruited nurses and doctors at the hospital. She sat him down in her living room, settled opposite him with a notebook, and her face changed. No more smiles, no more cakes. A real head of human resources.

"Monsieur Popescu," she began in an icy voice, "why should we choose you rather than another candidate?" Radu stammered. He talked about Lyon, his sister, the Fourvière room, Lucia, the țambal, all at the same time. Odile noted something down without saying anything. Then she asked the next question.

After an hour, she closed her notebook. "You talk too much," she said. "You answer three questions when you’re asked one. And you say ’super’ every two minutes. But you have something many candidates don’t: it’s obvious you love what you do."

She gave him three pieces of advice. Breathe before each answer. Never speak badly of anyone. And for the question about weaknesses, be honest, but show that you’re working on correcting them. "Recruiters don’t like perfect candidates," she added. "They don’t believe them."

On Sunday evening, Radu ironed his only white shirt. He ironed it three times, because he made a new crease with each attempt. Lucia ended up doing it herself, sighing. Then he prepared a folder with his best drawings, printed on good paper, in chronological order.

Right on top of the pile he put a drawing he had made the week before, almost without thinking: a small music room for the school in La Duchère. A simple wooden room with big windows, walls that absorb sound, and a corner for storing the plastic buckets.

On Monday, the interview went better than he had hoped. He breathed before each answer. He said "super" only twice. When Nathalie brought up favouritism, he answered calmly, as Odile had taught him. And when she asked the question about weaknesses, he was honest.

At the end, Nathalie leafed through his folder in silence. She stopped for a long time at the last drawing, the La Duchère one. She asked whether it was a project for the school of architecture. Radu said no, it was just an idea, for Julien’s children. Nathalie said nothing. But she kept the drawing.

Meanwhile, Ioana suspected nothing. Or rather, she was pretending. For a week she had found her brother strangely calm and polite. He no longer ate with his fingers. He had bought a tie. And Lucia had asked her, casually, how to say "point faible" in Romanian.

On Tuesday, another piece of news arrived, less cheerful. Hélène had caught a bad cold. Nothing serious, the doctor had said, but at her age one had to be careful. She had to stay in her room for a week, which put her in a very bad mood. Madame Lambert brought her herbal teas and crosswords.

Julien went to see her on Wednesday, as always. She was sitting in her armchair, wrapped in a blanket, her nose red. "I’ll be at the concert on 14 December," she declared before he had even said hello. "The doctor can say what he likes. I didn’t collect three hundred signatures to stay in bed."

Julien smiled, but he noticed she looked more tired than usual. Her hands were thinner, her voice a little weaker. He read her the newspaper for an hour, as she liked. When he left, she had fallen asleep, her head tilted to one side, a smile on her lips.

On Friday at noon, Radu’s phone rang. He was in the middle of a structures class, among thirty students. He ran out into the corridor. It was Nathalie. Her voice was as formal as ever: "Monsieur Popescu, I am pleased to inform you that your application has been successful."

Radu shouted so loudly that the teacher came out to see what was going on. Nathalie waited for him to calm down, then added, in a normal voice this time: "I’ll be honest with you, Radu. Technically, another candidate was better than you. Chloé, a student from Grenoble. I’ve taken her too."

"But what made up my mind," she went on, "was your La Duchère drawing. I showed it to Claire Vasseur yesterday. If the region votes the budget, she’d like to build a real rehearsal room in the neighbourhood. And she’s looking for someone to do the first sketches. You start on 8 January."

Radu stood motionless in the corridor, phone in hand, long after the call had ended. A student walking past asked if he was all right. Radu looked at him with shining eyes and replied, very seriously: "Please accept, sir, the expression of my most distinguished joy."

In the evening, he arrived at Ioana’s with Lucia, a bottle of wine and a bouquet of flowers that was far too big. Ioana opened the door with Rose-Hélène in her arms. Before Radu could even open his mouth, she said: "Congratulations, Mr Intern." Radu stood open-mouthed. "How do you know? Did Nathalie tell you?"

"Nobody told me anything," Ioana replied, laughing. "But a brother who buys a tie, irons his shirts and stops eating with his fingers is either getting married or going to a job interview. And I knew Lucia wouldn’t agree to marry you before you could paint a wall."

Lucia burst out laughing. Radu pretended to be offended for three seconds, then took his sister and his niece in his arms. Rose-Hélène grabbed his new tie and put it in her mouth. Julien, coming in from the kitchen, said that was her way of signing the contract.

The four of them had dinner, or rather the five of them, since Rose-Hélène demanded her share of every dish. At the end of the meal, Radu raised his glass. "To Nathalie, who judged me on my work. To Odile, who taught me to keep quiet. To Lucia, who corrected my mistakes. And to Ioana, who pretended not to know anything."

Everyone clinked glasses. Then Rose-Hélène, who had been watching her father for a while, held out her arms to him and said, very clearly, her very first word: "Pa-pa." There was absolute silence. Julien put down his glass. There were tears in his eyes.

"Well," said Radu, after a moment. "I think tonight I’m no longer the star." Ioana took a photo and sent it straight to Iași. The grandmother’s reply arrived two minutes later, in Romanian: "Bravo. Acum să învețe să spună «Buni»."

Madam, currently a first-year master’s student in architecture at the École nationale supérieure d’architecture de Lyon, I am writing to apply for a six-month internship at Atelier Rhône.
After a bachelor’s degree obtained in Iași, in Romania, I spent a year in France thanks to the Erasmus programme. During that year, I took part in several projects renovating old buildings.
It was the Salle Henri Bernard, at Fourvière, that made me want to join your team. I was struck by the way you designed a space that is both modern and welcoming, conceived for those who use it.
I am proficient in the main drawing software and I also draw by hand. I speak Romanian, French and English fluently. I am curious and rigorous, and I enjoy teamwork.
I would be very pleased to present my work to you at an interview. I would be grateful if you would kindly consider my application.
I look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully, Radu Popescu.
